note: Optional textures for the served copy. The single-file build has no assets folder and falls back to flat colour, so nothing here is required to play.
rule: Nothing generated may stand in for real map data. Everything left in here dresses the player, who has no real-world counterpart to fetch, so nothing invented is displacing anything measured.
generatedWith: Pixa (FLUX 2 Klein), prompted for seamless tileable material

kit.note: The character's own gear — drawn in every mode, because no provider on Earth publishes a photograph of your jacket.

model.note: Generated character mesh, TRELLIS.2 via Hugging Face, from the reference image the project keeps for it. This is the original generation — 49,359 triangles, 1024-pixel atlas — with the floor it was built standing on cut away and each boot capped, by tools/glb-unfloor.py; see groundNote. It was regenerated once at 1536 with a 2048 atlas and no floor at all, which is structurally the cleaner file, and this one is the better-looking figure, which is what it is judged on. 38,096 triangles, closed, no floor plane. Off by default: Settings -> Player -> Scanned player model.
model.rocketNote: Generated firework, TRELLIS.2 from a reference image, and regenerated at full quality once the daily quota came back. The first one shipped with a 256-pixel JPEG atlas - tools/glb-optimise.py was asked to halve and re-encode it to hold the file under a megabyte - and at the size it is actually held, a hand's width from the camera, that read as a smudge with no stripes in it. It also shipped with 21.8% of its edges open, because the clusterer keyed its weld on the texture coordinate as well as the cell so every chart boundary tore, and it carried a second picture declared image/png whose bytes are not a PNG at all - little-endian sixteen-bit numbers, a piece of geometry that ended up under an image entry, in the file from its first commit and decoded by nobody because no material named it. This one is 1024 pixels, PNG, kept exactly as the generator made it: texture size 0 means leave the pictures and the numbers alone and only cut the floor. The clusterer is fixed, tools/glb-prune.py drops what no material reads, and the self-test checks the mesh is closed, that every normal is unit length at the stride the file declares, and that every picture begins the way the format it claims begins and is one some material wants. 0.0% of its edges open, 42,587 normals all unit, 67,000 triangles and a 1.8 MB atlas. Off by default: Settings -> Player -> Scanned firework.
model.normalsNote: Both meshes shipped smudged black, and it was one fault in tools/glb-optimise.py rather than anything about the bake. glTF wants every vertex attribute aligned to four bytes, so three signed bytes of normal are written as four - correct, except the padding has to be declared as the bufferView's byteStride, and it was not. Undeclared means tightly packed, so every reader stepped three bytes at a time through data written four apart: the first normal right and each one after dragged a byte further out of place, mixing one vertex's z into the next one's x. Half of them arrived as directions of no particular length, and a short normal draws dark, which is why the smudges followed nothing you could see in the texture. The character's bytes were still all there, so declaring the stride recovered it exactly; the firework's were not, because tools/glb-heal.py had already read them the same wrong way and written the result down as floats, so its normals are recomputed from its own triangles instead. Both tools are fixed, tools/glb-normals.py does the repair, and the self-test now reads every mesh here the way a glTF reader reads it and refuses a single normal that is not unit length.
model.wingsNote: It was generated wearing a spread pair of feathered wings, and the game strapped an elytra on over the top of them - two pairs at once. Cutting the scan's off was tried and is in the history as a warning: every rule that took the feathers took a strip of sleeve with them or left a ruff across the shoulders that read as a backpack, and the weld needed to close the wound afterwards merged eight thousand vertices that shared a place but not a texture coordinate, which dragged the picture across the atlas at every chart boundary and covered a clean figure in cracks. They are better wings than the built sheet anyway. So they are kept and hinged: a joint each, folded on the same signal the built pair takes, and the built pair comes off while the scan is the body on screen.
model.riggedNote: It arrived as one fused surface with no skeleton, so it stood rigid while the built figure walked, and the firework hung in mid-air beside it - the hand a rocket is held in belongs to the built arm, and the scan's own hand had no reason to be near it. It is given a skeleton at load: the joints the built figure has, a shoulder and a hip each side, a neck, and one for each wing, laid out in exactly the numbers the built rig uses so the two are the same skeleton, with every vertex weighted to the four nearest so a shoulder bends instead of shearing. The shoulder needed a collarbone as well as a spine to hang off, or the arm claimed it and dragged the chest out with it. It was also on backwards from the day it was added - reconstructed facing +Z while the eyes, the toes and the shoulders of everything else in this project face -Z - so every photograph of it was the back of a head. And it was measured wrong: the wing tips reach higher than the crown, so scaling the bounding box to one unit made everybody an eighth shorter than the height they had set. The loader turns it, and measures the head.
model.faceNote: The generated head is a smooth egg - no eyes, no mouth, nothing on either side of it - and a head with no front is a figure you cannot tell the facing of at any distance, which is the same reason the built model has eyes at all. So it gets a drawn-on face: two eyes and one continuous smile, laid flat on the skull rather than stood off it, aimed rather than rotated onto it, and the smile built as a single ribbon because separate tiles on a curved surface either gap at their corners or fight each other for depth. It hangs off the head joint, so it turns when the head turns. Where the head *is* used to be two constants read off whichever body was shipping - and a body regenerated at a different resolution has a head of its own size in its own place, so both eyes ended up hanging in the air above the skull. The ball is measured now, from the vertices the head joint owns, and every dimension of the face is a fraction of that radius.
model.qualityNote: It shipped soft for a fortnight and that was this pipeline, not the generator. tools/glb-optimise.py halved the 1024-pixel atlas to 512 and re-encoded it as JPEG to hold the file under a megabyte: three quarters of the picture, plus what JPEG does to every hard edge - the mush along the sleeve seams, the smeared boot, the flat face. That trade is right for an asset everybody downloads and wrong for one that is off by default and never in the single-file build. Passing a texture size of 0 now means leave the pictures and the numbers exactly as they are and only take the floor out, which is how this file is made.
model.shadowNote: The strip of sleeve under each folded wing came back from the first generation with no light in it at all, because the reconstructor only ever saw the figure from outside: in a glide the arms swing and both unlit strips point at the camera, which was the pair of black gashes across the shoulders. tools/glb-repaint.py painted them from the lit texels of the same part of the same body, and that tool is kept for the same fault elsewhere. This bake does not have it: the reference was given a clean white background rather than a shaded one, and the atlas ships unrepainted.
model.soleNote: The boots used to come out with ragged notched toes, pale blue-grey wedges underneath and shading shards up the shins, and every one of those was a repair of the ground cut rather than anything wrong with the boots. They are closed, flat and shoe-shaped now - see groundNote. What is left is a sole of one flat colour rather than one carrying the tread the generator drew on the floor, which is the honest cost of there being no sole in the file to keep.
model.mantleNote: The scan wears its wings as a mantle: the membrane at their root lies right across the shoulders and the upper back, and that piece belongs to the collarbones rather than to the wing joints - measured, not assumed, from which joint owns which vertex: the wing bones reach no closer to the midline than 0.19 of the figure's height. So no wing angle moves it, and rendering the deployed wings at -0.4, 0, 0.3 and 0.62 radians moves that band not at all. What moves it is the arm, through whatever share of the arm's swing the collarbone takes - and that share is zero now. Whatever it takes, it takes by rotating the top of the torso, and the torso is the part of this figure that needs no help: the jacket has a shoulder line, lapels, a collar and a zip, and all four survive exactly as long as nothing turns them. At 0.45 the shoulders swelled into round pads; at 0.80 they hunched forward until the whole figure read as a ball from below. The self-test's chest-drag check passed at both - 0.7 cm and 1.2 cm on a figure one unit tall, inside a two-centimetre tolerance - so that check is a floor and not a verdict, and it was read as a verdict twice. At zero the chest moves 0.0 cm, because it is not asked to move: the scan is left as the generator made it and only the arms swing off it. The cost is that from directly overhead with the wings out the sleeve passes through the wing root - a diagnostic angle, against a torso that is on screen the whole time.
model.atlasNote: The atlas is the generator's own 1024-pixel PNG, byte for byte: not resized, not re-encoded, not repainted. The second picture in the file, a metal-roughness map, is dropped by tools/glb-prune.py --drop-metal-rough, because TRELLIS writes metallicFactor 1.0 with a map and the loader sets metalness to 0, roughness to a constant and both maps to null - a scanned jacket is not a mirror - so it was 660 KB fetched, decoded, uploaded to the GPU and never read.
model.groundNote: The reference image has the figure standing on a soft contact shadow, and a single-image reconstructor reads a shadow as surface, so the generator built a square plate under it - 11,412 triangles of floor, with the boots merged into its top face rather than having soles of their own. Every sole repair before this one was downstream of that: a rule that dropped level triangles in the bottom slice took the soles with the plate, an ear-clipping fill closed the holes it left, a flat colour was painted into a corner of the atlas for the fill to sample, and the boots still came out ragged, then pale, then covered in shading shards. tools/glb-unfloor.py drops the whole bottom band and closes each boot with a fan around its own rim, which is convex at that height so no ear clipping is needed. Keeping the plate's own shoe print was tried first and cannot be made clean: the print's triangles are the plate's triangles, they reach out past the boot, and no ring in the mesh separates the two - every rule tried left flat flaps of floor sticking out sideways, and tightening it tore holes in the print. The cap takes its colour from the print instead, at one texel: the middle of the largest print triangle, given to every cap vertex, so nothing is interpolated and no neighbouring chart can bleed in. 0 open edges, and 118 level triangles in the bottom centimetre against the plate's 10,933 - both checked by the self-test.
model.streakNote: A pale streak ran down the outside of one trouser leg, and finding it took four wrong answers worth writing down. It is not in the mesh: the same geometry in flat white, contrast stretched over the full range, is smooth there. It is not a distortion of the mapping: no triangle on the leg is stretched or squeezed by so much as a factor of three. It is not an outlier among the trouser's own texels either - every threshold that caught it also caught something real, the lit side of the leg at five centimetres of neighbourhood and the boots' turn-ups at two. And it is not gutter bleed: the ring outside the charts is the same brightness as the charts, once the rasteriser is turned the right way up. It looked like white gutter for a while because the first measurement of it had v flipped, which is also what made a padding pass fill the charts instead of the gutter and take the trousers' median from 22 to 2. What it is: this atlas is packed edge to edge, 34.7 per cent of it inside a chart and no gutter at all where two charts meet, and the trouser's chart is packed against pale ones. A coordinate on a chart's edge lands in a texel the boundary runs through, so the surface draws a hairline of the neighbour. Turning filtering off does not help - nearest still picks the texel the coordinate lands in - which is why the streak survived that test. tools/glb-inset.py moves every coordinate that sits on a chart's edge five texels inward along its own triangle, capped at a quarter of the way to the triangle's middle. The cap is the difference between working and not: five texels flat shrank the jacket's small charts far enough to show their own boundaries as hard-edged blocks, while the leg, whose charts are large, was still improving. Chart interiors are untouched, so nothing shifts inside a chart and no facet edges appear. One faint tick is left where the long streak was.

removed: There used to be a scenery group here — foliage.jpg and rock.jpg — for the generated world. That world is gone: nothing is drawn from invented map data any more, so the two textures had nothing left to dress and were deleted rather than left sitting in the download.
